cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
cards.definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and \(m(q)\) output-tree parameters, and an initial state \(q_{0}\) with \(m(q_{0})=0\). For each state q and input symbol \(\sigma\) of arity k there is at most one rule \(q(\sigma (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}),y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\to r\). The finite right-hand side follows the grammar \(r ::= y_{j} | \delta (r_{1},\ldots ,r_{l}) | q' (x_{i},r_{1},\ldots ,r_{m(q' )})\), with \(\delta\) an output symbol of arity l and \(1\le i\le k\). Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input \(\sigma (t_{1},\ldots ,t_{k})\), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call \(q'\) on the indicated child \(t_{i}\) with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.
cards.why: Locate the decidability boundary for equivalence of terminating recursive tree programs with copying and nested output parameters.

context_blocks.text: A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by \(b(y,y)\) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

Gallot and Maneth’s June 2025 paper decides shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. Shape preservation means that the output has the input’s ordered tree shape, although labels may change. This property concerns a transformation’s relation to its own input and does not decide equality of two arbitrary transformations.

Gallot, Lhote and Nguyên’s January 2026 revision decides polynomial size-to-height growth and computes its degree. Such a bound compares the height of the output tree with the number of input nodes. Two transformations can satisfy the same growth bound while differing in their output labels or branching, so growth classification is distinct from functional equivalence.

Dartois, Nguyên and Peyrat’s May 2026 paper characterizes a class of functions of linear size-to-height increase using tree-to-tree Hennie machines and a typed lambda calculus. Its equivalence proof concerns the expressive power of two models. It is not an algorithm for deciding whether two arbitrary macro tree transducers produce identical outputs. Keeping these senses of equivalence separate prevents a misleading reading of the recent abstract.

A resolution would locate an important boundary of automatic program comparison. These programs already terminate and have a disciplined recursive structure, but still support nested parameter passing and copying. Decidability would provide a foundation for validating transformations and optimizations in that model; undecidability would demonstrate that structural recursion alone does not make full semantic equality effectively recognizable.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
cards.formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, on every pair of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes G,H over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether their possibly infinite value trees are exactly equal, including divergence leaves?
cards.definitions: Types are generated by o and \(\tau \to \sigma\). A terminal a of rank r has type \(o\to \cdots \to o\) with r arguments. A scheme has finitely many typed nonterminals, a start S:o, and exactly one rule \(F x_{1}\cdots x_{k}\to t\) for each \(F:\tau _{1}\to \cdots \to \tau _{k}\to o\). The distinct parameters \(x_{i}\) have the indicated types; t:o is a well-typed applicative term made from terminals, nonterminals and those parameters. There is no pattern matching, test on constructor values, nondeterministic choice, or restriction called safety. To obtain the value at a node, unfold the head nonterminal with substitution until a terminal a is exposed, then repeat for its r ordered arguments. If no terminal is ever exposed, that node is a nullary ⊥ leaf. This defines a tree over the alphabet extended with ⊥. Equality means identical node domains and labels at every finite address in the ordered tree; evaluation-step counts are ignored. The order of o is 0 and \(ord(\tau \to \sigma )=\max\)(\(ord(\tau )+1,ord(\sigma )\)); the maximum nonterminal order is finite but part of the input. Inputs may have different orders. No time bound is imposed beyond halting on every valid pair.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer is a single effective decision procedure for all finite input orders, with a proof of termination and correctness on equal as well as unequal trees. A negative answer proves this decision problem undecidable. Decidable model checking of one generated tree, a bounded-order subclass, or a conditional reduction to another open problem is not a full resolution.
cards.why: A fundamental decidability boundary for comparing higher-order recursive computations: expressive tree generators admit strong verification procedures, while exact equality of two generated behaviors remains unresolved.

cards.status_note: Open for unrestricted finite-order deterministic schemes with the exact tree semantics stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Conditional Horn reductions, model checking, probabilistic termination and higher-order polyregular functional equivalence do not by themselves settle it.

context_blocks.text: A finite recursive program can describe an infinite object without listing its nodes. The rule \(S\to a S\), for unary a, describes an endless chain of a labels. The two-rule system \(S\to a T\) and \(T\to a S\) describes exactly the same chain even though its internal call structure differs. This card asks whether such equality of the entire observable unfolding can always be decided when functions may also be passed as arguments.

The output is an uninterpreted constructor tree. A binary constructor named plus is merely a label with two ordered children; the model does not add the arithmetic equation \(plus(0,x)=x\). Likewise, it does not include a program context allowed to inspect generated values. This narrow semantics matters because equivalence questions for richer programming languages can be undecidable for reasons absent from recursion schemes.

Divergence is also observable in a precise way. The rule \(S\to S\) generates ⊥, while \(S\to a S\) generates an infinite productive chain. A scheme \(S\to b S c\), with binary b and nullary c, can expose infinitely many labels despite never completing its left subtree. Head unfolding therefore differs from an evaluation convention that insists on fully evaluating every argument before producing a constructor.

At order zero, the generated trees are regular and equality can be checked by comparing finite state descriptions. At order one, the problem connects to deterministic pushdown-language equivalence, whose decidability follows from Sénizergues’s theorem. Allowing higher-order parameters makes the finite description much more expressive. The inherited Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre paper identifies equivalence as a central remaining question.

That paper’s positive equivalence theorem concerns two kinds of representation: higher-order recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata generate the same tree class, with effective translations. It transfers the problem to language equivalence for deterministic collapsible pushdown automata. It does not give an algorithm that compares arbitrary trees represented in either formalism. The difference between representation equivalence and instance equivalence is essential here.

Powerful properties of a single tree are nevertheless decidable. Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre provide effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for monadic second-order logic and the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Reflection can enrich node labels with the truth of a chosen logical property. Having this machinery does not automatically turn two unrelated infinite descriptions into one object in the same decidable class on which all corresponding nodes can be compared.

Jochems supplies a route through coinductive higher-order constrained Horn clauses. The translation represents the generated tree using predicates interpreted through a greatest model and creates separate positive and negative instances. A suitable semidecision procedure for the resulting coinductive problems would yield a decision procedure by interleaving the two searches. The needed semidecidability is left open, so this is a reduction rather than a completed decision algorithm.

The same work handles divergence constructively: it transforms a scheme so that each ⊥ leaf is replaced by an infinite chain over a fresh unary symbol. Equality is preserved and reflected. Thus treating divergence carefully need not restrict the question to an informal assumption that every program is productive. The present formulation keeps divergence explicit so readers can compare two given schemes without an unstated promise.

Recent results with similar terminology concern other targets. Bojańczyk–Fabiański–Stefański’s April 2026 undecidability theorem compares functions at higher-order types in the polyregular \(\lambda\)-calculus, a language with list-processing operations and extensional input/output semantics. Its theorem is not a stated undecidability result for the closed constructor-tree generators defined above. No reduction identifying the two decision problems is assumed here.

Dal Lago–Fiorillo–Pistone’s LICS 2026 work instead decides almost-sure termination for a typed subclass of probabilistic recursion schemes, using algebraic generating functions. That achievement concerns termination probabilities under additional type restrictions. The inherited question asks exact equality of deterministic value trees at unrestricted finite orders, and remains separate.

cards.definitions: An automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a finite nonempty alphabet Σ, initial and final weight functions ι,τ:Q→ℤ∪{+∞}, and a transition weight δ:Q×Σ×Q→ℤ∪{+∞}. A weight +∞ marks an unavailable transition or endpoint. For w=a₁⋯a_m and a state sequence q₀,…,q_m, the run cost is ι(q₀)+Σ_{j=1}^m δ(q_{j−1},a_j,q_j)+τ(q_m), with +∞ absorbing under addition. Define A(w) as the minimum of these costs over all state sequences. For the empty word this is min_q(ι(q)+τ(q)); the minimum of no finite costs is +∞. There are no epsilon transitions, so each run consumes exactly one symbol per transition. Deterministic means that at most one state has finite initial weight and that for every state and input symbol at most one outgoing transition has finite weight. The candidate D may have different states, transitions and integer weights; equivalence requires D(w)=A(w), including agreement at +∞, for every w∈Σ*. Inputs explicitly list the finite sets and weight tables, using signed binary integers and a distinguished infinity symbol. The decision algorithm must terminate on every valid input, rejecting malformed encodings. The all-accepting and unweighted-endpoint presentation used in the main proof is linked to this endpoint-weighted presentation by Remark 8.1 and Appendix B of the cited full paper.
cards.answer_criterion: The original target requires decidability of this language of automata, or a proof of undecidability. It has been settled positively by the cited theorem. Decidability does not mean every weighted automaton is determinizable.

context_blocks.text: This historical question is resolved. Almagor, Arbel and Sheinvald prove that an algorithm can decide whether a min-plus weighted automaton has an equivalent deterministic one. The result appeared as a 2025 preprint and at SODA 2026; a July 2026 follow-up gives a primitive-recursive upper bound on the decision complexity.

A weighted automaton reads a word and accumulates costs along each possible run. Min-plus semantics adds costs along a run, then chooses the smallest total among competing runs. This represents an optimal cost rather than only a yes/no acceptance answer.

For example, one branch can count the a symbols and another the b symbols. Taking the minimum computes min(#a,#b) for every word. Which branch gives the final minimum can change after a long suffix, and this function has no equivalent deterministic weighted automaton. The theorem decides when a deterministic equivalent exists; it does not say that one always does.

The ordinary Boolean subset construction only needs to remember which states remain possible. Here different ways of reaching a state may carry different integer costs. A finite set of original states therefore does not by itself give a finite set of quantitative configurations. This is why eliminating nondeterminism is a separate decision problem.

The 2022 source specifically left unrestricted ambiguity open after results for machines with only polynomially many runs. The later theorem covers the general case. Its model-variant discussion includes initial and final weights, so restricting the displayed proof to all-accepting automata does not leave the historical question unanswered.

The exact optimal running-time complexity is a different question. The 2025 decidability proof did not give a complexity bound, while the LICS 2026 result establishes a primitive-recursive one. This record retains its original decidability target and is hidden from the active reader as resolved.

cards.definitions: A full binary tree is a map t:{L,R}*→Σ for a finite nonempty alphabet Σ; the empty word is the root. Specifying labels at k distinct nodes has probability |Σ|^{−k}; these cylinder probabilities determine the completed product measure. An automaton is a finite tuple (Σ,Q,q₀,Δ,Ω), with states Q, initial state q₀, transitions Δ⊆Q×Σ×Q×Q, and integer priorities Ω:Q→{0,…,d−1}. A run ρ assigns a state to every node, starts at q₀, and satisfies (ρ(v),t(v),ρ(vL),ρ(vR))∈Δ. It accepts if on every infinite branch the largest priority appearing infinitely often is even. A tree belongs to L(A) if there exists such an accepting run; the random choices generate the input tree, not a run. All finite tables are given explicitly, with integers in binary. Exact output may be a first-order formula over (R,0,1,+,×,≤) with one free real variable whose unique satisfying value is the required probability; real quantifiers and polynomial equalities and inequalities have their usual meanings. The result ensures this value is algebraic. For the branching-process extension, an input finite alphabet has an arity assigned to each label. A finite set of process states has an initial state, and each state carries a rational probability distribution on finitely many tuples (a,r₁,…,rₛ), where s is the arity of a. At a node in that state, an independent draw chooses its label and the states of its ordered children. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded. The automaton uses transitions (q,a,q₁,…,qₛ), with the same parity condition on every infinite branch and a valid transition at each leaf. The task is the probability that the resulting, possibly finite, tree admits an accepting run.
cards.answer_criterion: A uniform terminating exact-measure algorithm for every finite parity tree automaton, including the rational branching-process input variant, answers the source question affirmatively. No weak or deterministic acceptance restriction is allowed. Exact output must identify the measure uniquely and permit comparison with rational thresholds; numerical estimates or the measurability theorem alone are insufficient. The source asks for computability, without a target optimal running time.

cards.title: Collapse versus arbitrary higher-order stacks
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved positively: is there a language of finite words recognized by a deterministic collapsible higher-order pushdown automaton that no deterministic noncollapsible pushdown automaton of any finite order recognizes? The quantifier over competing noncollapsible automata ranges over every finite order, with no bound on their state or stack alphabets.
cards.why: Shows that adding more ordinary nesting levels cannot replace the link-based collapse operation in deterministic language recognition. The separation also distinguishes general higher-order recursion schemes from the safe hierarchy used to model restricted higher-order computation.

cards.definitions:
Fix finite input and stack alphabets. An order-one stack is a finite nonempty list of stack symbols; an order-\(j\) stack is a finite nonempty list of order-\((j-1)\) stacks. The top is the last element, recursively. An order-\(r\) automaton has finite control and one order-\(r\) stack, initially containing a single symbol at every nesting level.

In the journal's equivalent stack convention, \(\mathrm{pop}_j\) removes the top order-\((j-1)\) component of the top order-\(j\) stack, and is undefined if it would empty that stack. The operation \(\mathrm{push}^{\gamma}_j\) duplicates its top order-\((j-1)\) component and replaces the top symbol of the new copy by \(\gamma\). For \(j=1\), this simply appends a symbol. Operations apply along the recursively topmost chain; arbitrary interior components are inaccessible. The source notes that allowing symbol replacement on higher-order duplication does not change expressive power.

A transition is fixed by the control state and visible top symbol. It either performs one stack operation without reading input, or reads the next input letter and changes state according to a fixed letter-to-state map. These two modes do not compete nondeterministically. The journal uses injective letter-to-state maps, obtainable by splitting states. A finite word is accepted when a finite run from the initial configuration consumes exactly that word and ends in an accepting state. Silent transitions are allowed; infinite silent computation does not itself constitute acceptance. There is no time or stack-size bound.

For the order-two collapsible witness model, each stack symbol additionally carries a hidden positive integer. A first-order push records the current number of first-order stacks; a second-order duplication preserves the recorded integers. Control can inspect the symbol, but cannot read or perform arithmetic on its integer. If the top symbol stores \(h\), collapse discards top first-order stacks until exactly \(h-1\) remain; an empty resulting stack is invalid. The integer on the initial symbol can be set to one. This is the source's order-two collapse convention. The ordinary competing automata have no such links or collapse operation.

The theorem supplies a finite-alphabet witness. Write \(w\) over opening brackets, closing brackets and a star symbol. Let \(s(w)=0\) if some prefix has more closing than opening brackets, or if the total opening and closing counts are equal. Otherwise match brackets in the usual nested way and let \(s(w)\) count the stars strictly before the last unmatched opening bracket. With a new sharp symbol \(\#\), the journal uses
\[
U=\{\,w\#^{s(w)+1}:w\in\{\text{[},\text{]},\star\}^*\,\}.
\]
The alphabet is finite and carries no external data values. This adapted witness is defined in the later paper; it should not be confused with the bracket-only witness in the original order-two result.
cards.answer_criterion: The positive historical resolution requires one finite-word language accepted by a deterministic collapsible automaton, together with a proof that no deterministic noncollapsible automaton of any finite order accepts it. The journal’s Theorem 1.2 supplies both parts. Separation only from order-two competitors, from one fixed higher order, or in an infinite-data alphabet model would be insufficient.
